name: Abbey
lede: Abbey is a vivid blue-violet that appears in Maerz and Paul's 1930 color dictionary, with no recorded reason for its name.

sections.title: A name with no recorded reason
sections.body:
Abbey is a saturated blue-violet, #6457AE, and the only source that records it in our library is Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, which lists it as first recorded in 1921 on plate 41, position F 10 [1]. The dictionary's reason for the name is not in our collection, so the origin is undocumented.

In the concordance of our 29 books, the word turns up only as a building, never as a color [7].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch is a screen approximation of a color printed on a plate in 1930 [1]. It measures about 42 in lightness and 53 in chroma, at a hue angle near 301 degrees, which is a blue-violet [6]. The nearest named color in our app is [[purple]], 9.6 units away, so it sits between [[royal-blue]] and purple, nearer to [[periwinkle]] than to [[indigo]] [6].

sections.title: Abbeys in the color books
sections.body:
The books put abbeys beside color for two reasons. Suger rebuilt the abbey church of Saint-Denis near Paris in the 1130s and 1140s as what Pastoureau calls a temple of color, and St Clair credits its craftsmen with perfecting cobalt-colored glass [2][3]. In the same books, the black of monks and clerics stands for humility and temperance [2].

The second is Merton Abbey in Surrey, where William Morris had his dye works [3]. Visitors watched wool come out of woad vats an almost grassy color before it turned blue in the air [3], and Morris recorded his indigo discharge recipes in a Merton Abbey dye book [4].

Neither of these blues is the swatch, and no book says Maerz and Paul had them in mind [1][3]. They are places to see blues made by hand [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Abbey, matched within six units of CIEDE2000 and covering at least five per cent of the canvas, appears in only 2 of 23,781 paintings in our archive [5]. They are Edvard Munch's *Forest on the Way to Borre* of 1901 and John Singer Sargent's *Bedouins* of 1905, covering 14 and 11 per cent [5]. Both date from the first years of the twentieth century [5]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is not a pigment test [5].

Where to look: [[painter:edvard-munch|Munch]]'s [[painting:commons-Q18889878|Forest on the Way to Borre]] holds the color across 14 per cent of the canvas [5].
